Evolution of cortical neurons supporting human cognition

How many cell types? Single-cell transcriptomics now makes it possible to count cell types at whole-brain scale. A census of the adult human brain sequenced more than three million nuclei from about 100 dissections across three donors and grouped them into 31 superclusters, 461 clusters, and 3,313 subclusters of neurons and non-neuronal cells. The hierarchy largely followed developmental origin, and much of the neuronal diversity was in the midbrain and hindbrain rather than the cortex 2. A whole-mouse-brain atlas combining single-cell RNA sequencing with spatial transcriptomics found 34 classes, 338 subclasses, 1,201 supertypes, and 5,322 clusters, of which 5,205 were neuronal. Most clusters were confined to specific brain regions, so this molecular diversity is organized anatomically rather than scattered randomly 3. These numbers count transcriptomic clusters, not established functional types. Where morphology and electrophysiology have been measured in the same cells, the number of distinguishable types is smaller; for example, mouse visual cortex GABAergic interneurons sort into about 28 morpho-electric-transcriptomic types 4. A lifespan-spanning human brain cell atlas unifies data from nine studies (Figure). Cell types show different rates of molecular maturation toward adult identity (Figure).

Shape and firing vary across types: transcriptomic types also differ in the two properties classical neuroanatomy and electrophysiology originally used to define cell types, namely dendritic and axonal morphology and intrinsic firing. Patch-seq measures all three in the same cell: it records a neuron’s electrophysiology, fills it with dye to reconstruct its morphology, and then sequences its RNA. Across more than 1,200 Patch-seq neurons in mouse motor cortex, morphology ranged from compact interneurons with dense local axons to pyramidal cells whose dendrites span the cortical depth, and firing ranged from fast, non-adapting spike trains to strongly adapting ones. Morpho-electric properties differed sharply between broad transcriptomic families but varied mostly continuously among types within a family, so molecular, anatomical, and physiological identity line up only partly 5. In human cortex, layer 2/3 pyramidal neurons, which look fairly uniform in mouse, split into transcriptomic types with distinct dendritic shapes, sag currents, and firing adaptation, and these types are more distinct from each other than their mouse counterparts are. This suggests that the expansion of human supragranular cortex came with diversification of its excitatory neurons 6. Patch-seq reconstructions and voltage traces show the morphological and electrophysiological range of mouse cortical neuron types (Figure). Human supragranular pyramidal neuron types differ visibly in dendritic morphology and intrinsic electrophysiology (Figure). This recent connectomic study adds synapse-scale anatomical detail (Figure) 9. This recent connectomic study adds synapse-scale anatomical detail (Figure).

Gene expression is not the whole story: cells with the same transcriptomic identity can still differ in morphology, connectivity, and function. In the larval zebrafish optic tectum, more than 60 transcriptomic neuron types are arranged in distinct layers, yet within a single type, dendritic shape, connectivity, and visual tuning vary systematically with the cell’s position in the tectum 7. Spatial position can therefore add functional diversity inside a molecularly defined type, which means a full description of cell identity has to combine expression, morphology, physiology, connectivity, and location.

Evolution reshapes the palette: a comparative atlas of more than 1.3 million cells from the telencephalon and cerebellum of turtles, zebra finches, pigeons, mice, and macaques found both conserved and species-specific populations, with the largest differences between birds and mammals in telencephalic excitatory neurons and cerebellar cell types. One example is an SVIL-positive Purkinje cell subtype found only in birds, a new variant within one of the most conserved neuron classes. The authors attribute much of this diversification to divergence or loss of duplicated (paralogous) genes 8. The mouse whole-brain atlas provides a visual overview of how molecular cell identity relates to anatomy and neurotransmitter class (Figure).

Diversity and characterization of excitatory neurons (diversity of topologies, firing patterns, etc etc)

Pyramidal cells of each layer of cortex; fit for the heterarchical predictive coding characteristic of cortex

At the apex of cortical processing sit the excitatory, glutamatergic projection neurons that constitute roughly 80% of cortical cells. Classic Golgi and modern connectomic data converge on three canonical families: intratelencephalic (IT) neurons that interconnect cortical areas, corticothalamic (CT) neurons that close cortex-thalamus loops, and pyramidal-tract (PT) neurons that descend to brainstem and spinal cord. Pyramidal neurons serve as the brain’s primary excitatory units and information integrators, featuring elaborate dendritic trees with up to 10,000 synapses each, enabling them to perform complex nonlinear computations before signals even reach the soma; their apical dendrites extend across cortical layers, allowing them to integrate feedforward sensory information with top-down predictions. Layer-specific variants range from the compact, locally projecting spiny stellate cells of layer 4 to the gigantic Betz cells of layer 5 that synchronise fast motor output. A striking specialisation unique to large-brained mammals is the von Economo (spindle) neuron, a fusiform, bifurcating projection cell concentrated in the anterior cingulate and fronto-insular cortices and implicated in rapid, long-range integration of interoceptive and social information. [citation needed]

Diversity and characterization of inhibitory neurons (diversity of topologies, firing patterns, etc etc)

Balancing cortical excitation is an intricately tiered menagerie of GABAergic interneurons, numerically fewer yet functionally indispensable. Parvalbumin-positive (PV+) interneurons fire at rates exceeding 200 Hz and create precise temporal windows for computation through feedforward inhibition. Somatostatin-positive (SST+) interneurons selectively target pyramidal dendrites, implementing gain control and feature selection. Vasoactive intestinal peptide (VIP+) interneurons primarily inhibit other interneurons, creating disinhibitory circuits that gate learning and attention-a biological attention mechanism predating transformers by 500 million years. [citation needed]

Diversity and characterization of neuromodulatory neurons (diversity of topologies, firing patterns, etc etc)

A third axis of diversity is neuromodulatory neurons, whose sparse but far-reaching axons reconfigure whole networks on behavioural time-scales. Dopaminergic neurons in the ventral tegmental area and substantia nigra encode prediction errors; noradrenergic locus-coeruleus neurons broadcast salience; serotonergic raphe neurons convey behavioural context; cholinergic basal-forebrain neurons toggle encoding versus consolidation modes; and histaminergic tuberomammillary neurons regulate arousal. Even within a class such as the noradrenergic neurons of the locus coeruleus, transcriptomics resolves multiple projection-biased subtypes, demonstrating that modulatory populations are not homogeneous broadcast units but finely tuned control ensembles. [citation needed]

Diversity and characterization of particularly specialized neurons (diversity of topologies, firing patterns, etc etc)

Many brain regions harbour idiosyncratic neuron types that embody specialised computations. The cerebellum’s Purkinje cells represent nature’s most extreme dendritic computers, with each cell receiving inputs from up to 200,000 parallel fibers while outputting through a single axon-the ultimate fan-in architecture. These cells implement error-driven learning through climbing fiber inputs that trigger complex spikes, providing teaching signals at precisely 1-2 Hz; this architecture enables the cerebellum to contain over half the brain’s neurons while occupying only 10% of its volume. The basal ganglia revolves around dopamine-responsive medium spiny neurons that come in D1 (direct) and D2 (indirect) flavours to orchestrate action selection. Hippocampal place-field coding emerges from CA1 and CA3 pyramidal neurons coupled to dentate gyrus granule and mossy cells, while thalamic relay versus reticular neurons form the core of attentional gating loops. Sensory peripheries add their own specialities-retinal ganglion cells include  30 types, each encoding specific visual features like motion direction, edges, or color opponency; cochlear hair cells achieve mechanical-to-electrical transduction with sub-nanometer precision; olfactory neurons each express one of  400 receptor types, implementing a sparse coding scheme that can discriminate over a trillion odors. This illustrates the brain’s strategy of embedding domain-specific front-ends into a common cortical representational substrate. [citation needed]

Another idiosyncrasy is the von Economo neurons-large, spindle-shaped cells found only in humans, great apes, elephants, and cetaceans. Concentrated in the anterior cingulate and frontoinsular cortex, these neurons have minimal dendritic branching but project across vast distances, potentially implementing rapid, long-range communication for social cognition and self-awareness. [citation needed]

Diversity and characterization of regional neuronal specializations

Across the cortex, evolutionary and activity-dependent pressures have sculpted region-specific repertoires of neuronal subtypes whose biophysics, morphology, and gene expression are tuned to the computations those regions perform. In primary sensory areas, for example, layer IV spiny stellate cells in the barrel cortex relay whisker deflections with sub-millisecond fidelity, while V1’s layer II/III pyramidal neurons form elongated axonal arbors that integrate oriented edge information across neighboring columns. Motor cortex, by contrast, is enriched in thick-tufted corticospinal pyramidal neurons with high-density Kv3 channels that sustain the rapid, high-gain burst firing needed for precise movement initiation. Prefrontal cortex sports a disproportionately large population of chandelier and Martinotti interneurons whose powerful, target-specific inhibition sculpts persistent activity and working-memory circuits, and it uniquely contains von Economo neurons that couple long-range social and interoceptive signals. Even ostensibly "canonical" inhibitory classes fragment into region-adapted subtypes: vasoactive-intestinal-peptide (VIP) interneurons in auditory belt cortex show broader frequency tuning and stronger nicotinic excitation than their visual-cortex counterparts, matching the demands of rapid gain control in a temporally dynamic modality. Transcriptomic atlases now catalog well over 100 glutamatergic and 60 GABAergic cell types, revealing gradients in ion-channel, neuromodulator, and adhesion-molecule expression that precisely mirror each region’s temporal integration window, plasticity rules, and long-range connectivity pattern. [citation needed]

What was once catalogued by Nissl stain and silver chromate impregnation is now charted in high-dimensional molecular space. These atlases reveal that cell-type identity is not a flat list but a hierarchical coordinate in a five-dimensional space of gene expression, morphology, electrophysiology, projection pattern and developmental lineage. Such structured diversity allows the brain to allocate distinct learning rules, plasticity mechanisms and dynamical regimes to different components of its world model-for example, fast spike-timing-dependent plasticity in parvalbumin-expressing GABAergic interneurons, eligibility-trace-based reinforcement in dopamine-targeted striatal neurons, and multistage consolidation in corticothalamic loops. [citation needed] Spatial transcriptomics maps developing cell types onto cortical layers (Figure) 10.
